title: Quentin and the Winter
premise: August Whitlock, a hospice nurse who hears the dying count backwards toward something, inherits their grandmother's house and discovers every photograph now contains an extra empty chair—and the chair is moving closer in each image. The counting they hear at bedsides is the same countdown the house's previous residents heard before the winter of 1974, when a bargain was struck: a child given to the cold in exchange for the town's survival. August learns their grandmother took that child's place by theft, not sacrifice, and the debt has come due. To end it, August must return what was taken—a locket holding the stolen name—before the harvest moon rises, choosing truth over loyalty to grandma's memory and love over the duty of staying alive.
about_author: Casper Brightwater spent a decade working night shifts in long-term care facilities across rural New England, where he collected the last words of strangers in a series of waterlogged notebooks. He writes from a farmhouse with too many chairs.

chapters.title: The Counting Ward
chapters.summary: August Whitlock, hospice nurse, documents patients' final days in meticulous journals. Three dying patients in one week count backwards from ten, stopping at zero with identical smiles. POV: August. Emotional beat: professional detachment beginning to crack into dread.

chapters.title: Probate and Porridge
chapters.summary: August moves into grandma Edith's inherited house to settle the estate. The kitchen smells of porridge no one cooked; a fourth place setting appears at the table overnight. POV: August. Emotional beat: grief tangled with unease.

chapters.title: An Extra Chair
chapters.summary: Sorting photo albums, August finds an empty wooden chair in every picture after 1974—closer to the camera in each successive decade. In the newest photos it sits beside them. POV: August. Emotional beat: denial curdling into certainty.

chapters.title: Documentation Is a Kind of Prayer
chapters.summary: August photographs the chair obsessively, logging times and positions. The chair appears in real time now, always just outside reach, always facing them. A neighbor warns them to stop looking. POV: August. Emotional beat: compulsion versus self-preservation.

chapters.title: Mrs. Halloran Counts Down
chapters.summary: August's patient Mrs. Halloran counts backwards for six hours, whispering names August doesn't know, ending with 'the Whitlock girl.' She dies smiling as frost blooms on the hospital window in July. POV: August. Emotional beat: horror becoming personal.

chapters.title: Edith's Locked Room
chapters.summary: August breaks open grandma's locked attic room: children's clothes from 1974, newspaper clippings about a missing girl named Wren Calloway, and a cold spot shaped like a small body. POV: August. Emotional beat: betrayal of a beloved memory.

chapters.title: The Winter That Didn't End
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, 1974, from young Edith's perspective: the harshest winter in memory, a figure called the Tithe-Man walking the frozen fields, and the town's desperate bargain. POV: Edith (past). Emotional beat: fear dressed up as duty.

chapters.title: What Was Taken
chapters.summary: Back in the present, August finds Edith's confession hidden in a hymnal: Wren was chosen by lot, but Edith stole her locket—the vessel of her name—and hid, so the Tithe-Man took nothing and the debt stayed open. POV: August. Emotional beat: loyalty to grandma shattering against truth.

chapters.title: The Town Remembers Differently
chapters.summary: August interviews elderly locals who insist Edith 'saved us all.' Their stories contradict the confession. One man, drunk, admits he drew the black stone and let Edith take his place in the lottery. POV: August. Emotional beat: complicity everywhere.

chapters.title: Frost in July
chapters.summary: Cold spreads from the house outward—killed garden, frosted well, breath visible indoors. The chair now sits at the foot of August's bed each morning. The counting starts inside the walls. POV: August. Emotional beat: siege.

chapters.title: Wren
chapters.summary: August dreams in 1974 through Wren's eyes: her last day, her mother sewing her coat pocket shut so she couldn't carry anything away, her walk to the field line. POV: Wren (dream). Emotional beat: heartbreak; the victim becomes a person.

chapters.title: The Locket
chapters.summary: August locates the locket welded inside the old furnace, engraved with Wren's name, warm despite everything around it being frozen. Touching it, they hear ten... nine... eight. POV: August. Emotional beat: dread fused with resolve.

chapters.title: Dana Says Run
chapters.summary: August's partner Dana arrives, sees the frost and the chair, and begs August to abandon the house and the debt—it isn't theirs to pay. First open fight in years. POV: Dana. Emotional beat: love against duty.

chapters.title: The Tithe-Man's Terms
chapters.summary: The Tithe-Man appears at the property line, courteous and terrible, offering terms: return the locket and the debt transfers to the Whitlock bloodline—or keep it and the cold takes the whole county. POV: August. Emotional beat: impossible arithmetic.

chapters.title: Researching the Harvest Moon
chapters.summary: August digs through almanacs and church records: the debt comes due on the harvest moon, four nights away, when the field line opens. Previous attempts to return things ended badly—one family erased entirely. POV: August. Emotional beat: racing the calendar.

chapters.title: The Erased Family
chapters.summary: August finds the Hollis farm, unlisted on maps since 1979, its house still standing under permanent snow. Inside, dinner set for five, plates full and fossilized. They tried to run with a stolen thing. POV: August. Emotional beat: consequences made physical.

chapters.title: Zero
chapters.summary: Every dying patient in three counties begins counting backwards simultaneously. August, on shift, listens helplessly as a ward full of voices reaches zero together and the temperature drops ten degrees. POV: August. Emotional beat: guilt—the debt is everyone's now.

chapters.title: Choosing
chapters.summary: Night before the harvest moon. Dana offers to carry the locket themselves; August refuses. They reconcile not by agreeing but by deciding to face it together. August writes their own obituary, then burns it. POV: August. Emotional beat: love chosen freely, duty redefined.

chapters.title: The Field Line
chapters.summary: Harvest moonrise. August walks to the 1974 field boundary carrying the locket, the chair walking behind them step for step, the Tithe-Man waiting among standing corn turned to ice. POV: August. Emotional beat: terror transfigured into ceremony.

chapters.title: Return What Was Taken
chapters.summary: August refuses the terms: instead of transferring the debt, they speak Wren's full name back into the locket and give it—not to the Tithe-Man, but to the air, unowned. The bargain had never specified who received it. POV: August. Emotional beat: defiance as grace.

chapters.title: Thaw
chapters.summary: The Tithe-Man unravels without a claim to hold; the chair empties, whitens, becomes only wood, then ash. Frost retreats county-wide. Patients stop counting. But August keeps hearing a single voice say 'thank you' in a child's register. POV: August. Emotional beat: exhausted relief, tender aftermath.

chapters.title: Too Many Chairs
chapters.summary: Weeks later, August and Dana restore the house. August leaves one extra chair at every table forever—an offering, a memorial, a warning. Final photograph: the chairs are all empty, and stay that way. Mostly. POV: August. Emotional beat: peace that knows better than to be certain.
